speakerposition: topic
Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I beg to lay on the Table of the
House the authentic texts of the Draft Conventions and Recommendations adopted by the International Labour Conference (League of Nations) at its third session held in Geneva, Switzerland, October 25-November 19, 1921.
Under paragraph 5 of article 405 of the Treaties of Peace.
Each of the members undertakes that it will, within the period of one year at most from the closing of the session of the conference, or if it is impossible owing to exceptional circumstances ^to do so within the period of one year, then at the earliest practicable moment and in no case later than eighteen months from the closing of the session of the conference, bring the recommendation or draft convention before the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies, for the enactment of legislation 01-other, action.
When the authentic texts of the Draft Conventions and Recommendations of the '1921 conference were received from the Secretary-General o.f the League of Nations they were referred to the Department of Justice for
International Labour

consideration of the question whether the proposals involved were to be regarded as within Dominion or provincial legislative competent The report, of the Minister of Justice on this subject was approved by order in council on June 27, 1922, and a copy of the order in council is attached to the texts of the Draft Conventions and Recommendations for the information of the House. It will be observed that most of the proposals were found to be within provincial jurisdiction. Copies of the order in council of June 27, 1922, and of the authentic texts of the Draft Conventions and Recommendations were transmitted subsequently to the different lieutenant-governors for the consideration of their respective governments with a view to such legislative or other action in line with the proposals involved as each provincial government might be advised to take. The obligations of the government of Canada under the Peace Treaties have thus been fulfilled in respect of the individual measures of the 1921 conference which were found to be within the provincial sphere.
With respect to those Draft Conventions and Recommendations which were found to be within federal legislative competence, the authentic texts are being brought before parliament in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 5 of article 405 of the Treaties of Peace and are being laid on the Table of the House. The questions involved in these latter Draft Conventions and Recommendations are also receiving the attention of the government. The Dominion government has proposed to the several provincial governments, that a Dominion-provincial conference should be held for the purpose of considering certain aspects of matters arising out of the relations between Canada and the International Labour Organization. Most of the provinces have already expressed their acquiescence in this suggestion and it is expected that the meeting will be held in the early part of next summer.
Referring to the inquiry which was made in the House yesterday by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), as to "when the House may' expect the report of the last meeting of the International Labour Conference," I find that the government has not as yet received either the printed report of the discussions of the conference or the authentic texts of the recommendations which were adopted by the conference.
As I mentioned yesterday, a report of the 1922 session of the International Labour Conference appeared in the December issue of the Labour Gazette, the official monthly Journal of the Department of Labour of Canada. I have pleasure in laying a copy of a re-print

of this article from the Labour Gazette on the Table of the House for the purposes of information.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My information is that the report in the Gazette to which the hon. member referred yesterday and again to-day is not a complete report. It is only in part a report of the conference. Is that correct? I may not have caught what the hon. gentleman said, but I did not come to any clear understanding myself of his remarks as to why the report could be in the Gazette of December and the government not yet in receipt of the full report to lay on the Table of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
My hon. friend will note that I have only laid on the Table of the House the authentic text of the draft conventions adopted at the 1921 conference. The authentic text of what was done at the 1922 conference has not yet been received by the Department of Labour. It has not yet come to Canada. We hope to have it within the next few months; but there is always, I understand, great delay in sending forward the authentic text. The report that appeared in the issue of December last of the Labour Gazette was, it is believed, as full and complete as was necessary. I am going to send across the floor to my right hon. friend a copy so that he can peruse it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I observe in the press to-day an announcement that Mrs. James Carruthers of England, who formerly was Miss Violet Markham, has been selected to represent this government on the governing body of the International Labour Conference at its meeting in April. Is this correct, and if it is, what superior qualifications has she over Canadians to represent us on that body?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The report is correct, although I do not think it would be at all proper to intimate that Mrs. James Carruthers would have any superior qualifications over very many of our Canadian women. The circumstances are, however, that we received notice only very recently, as to the date of the next meeting of the governing body of the International Labour Office to be held on April 10 at Geneva, and with that notice a copy of the agenda of the matters to be dealt with. For the January meeting of the governing body, we received notice so late that it was regarded as inadvisable, under the circumstances,

Supply-Immigration
to endeavour to arrange for a substitute for the representative for Canada on the governing board for the January meeting. On this occasion, we undertook to secure representation hurriedly and by cable, endeavouring to secure a gentleman who, it was thought, would very ably represent Canada. That was found impossible; so Mrs. James Carruthers was asked to represent Canada and she very kindly consented to act. Mrs. Carruthers, although resident in England, has visited all parts of Canada, and is the author of a handbook on the Factory and Shop Acts of the British dominions, which was issued by the industrial sub-committee of the Victoria League. She is a member of the executive committee of the British National Relief Fund and of the Central Committee of Women's Employment, and was Deputy Director of the Women's section of the National Service Department in 1917, and was appointed a member of the British Industrial Court in 1920.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Just to save time, will the hon. gentleman lay on the Table of the House to-morrow, if possible, the notification, with notification of its receipt, and- the other correspondence to which he has just referred? I may mention that there was one qualification which he forgot, namely that this lady was a Liberal candidate for Parliament at the last election; running against the Labour candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I was uninformed as to that fact, if it is a fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

They are engaged on inspectional work, checking out any Chinese leaving the country, investigating each newcomer, taking care of deports, and a thousand and one other things in connection with the fairly numerous Chinese population of British Columbia. Frequent trips have to be taken inland in search of Chinese who have entered illegally, and this involves a considerable expenditure. My hon. friends from the coast are continually complaining of laxity on the part of our officials in prosecuting these cases, and I am free to say that I get a great many complaints. I do not think the staff is overmanned for the work that has to be done. True, if the bill which we will be discussing in a day or two is enacted into law practically only merchants and students will be allowed to enter. The work of our officials will then be confined to protecting the population against any

Chinese who come in illegally. Of course, I do not want to imply that that will be the sole business of the staff.
Perhaps the minister can tell us how many men he has on this work altogether. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

Of course, I do not doubt the minister's statement at all, but I understand that every boat reaching Yancouver from China carries quite a large number of Chinese children. This is another way in which the Chinese evade the regulations. We all know that the greater proportion of Chinese who seek admission claim to be merchants, and I think the minister will have a great deal of difficulty in defining a merchant in his bill, because the wily Chinese always finds a way to get around any restrictive regulations. The minister should be very careful in framing his definition. It will be a mistake if under his proposed bill merchants are allowed to enter to carry on business here permanently. Chinese merchants might be given permits to come in and carry on business temporarily, but we shall be faced with a very grave danger if we allow them to remain here permanently. ,1 would suggest to the minister that Chinese merchants who desire to live here permanently should be excluded, for if you allow a Chinaman to enter as a merchant you at once lose control over him and he can engage in any occupation that appeals to him. I think also the minister should insert a provision in his bill to deport students who remain in the country after they have finished their university courses. As the law now stands it appears that once a Chinese is admitted as a student he can engage in any occupation he chooses to take up and it is impossible to deport him. A Chinaman is supposed to have several wives, and we can readily believe this when we see so many Chinese children sent to this country to join their supposed parents here. I should like to hear from the minister what investigation is made in reference to such children and whether the department is able to ascertain beyond question that the large number ' who are now entering Canada are really the children of Chinese already resident here.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think perhaps my hon. friend knows more about the difficulties of controlling Chinese immigration than I do. I had a very bright Chinese boy in my office the other night, in fact as bright a Chinese lad as I have ever seen. He is here on permit, and his case has been under investigation for four weeks. A Chinaman here swears that he is the boy's father; and the boy swears that he is the son of the Chinaman.
How can he swear that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

Well, the boy is under twelve years of age, so perhaps it is not proper to say that he swears to the fact. But he alleges that he is the son of a Chinaman in Toronto. A number of Chi-

nese people in Toronto say they were in China at the date of the birth of this boy, and that he is really the son of the Chinaman referred to. We do not think he is. There is certain contradictory evidence which would indicate that perhaps this is a case where the complaint of my hon. friend is justified. I merely mention this incident to show the difficulties we are confronted with. Taking it by and large my hon. friend is right as to the large number of Chinese children being sent to this country. Once it became known that the bill I have referred to would be introduced a lot of Chinese nationals resident in Canada attempted to bring in their children from China before the bill became law, and frankly we are suspicious that many of these children are not really the offspring of the men who are endeavouring -to get them into this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

How are these Chinese sworn? The Chinese take two or three kinds of oaths in our courts. One is by breaking a saucer, another by burning a paper. The Chinaman writes his name on a piece of paper, sets fire to it, and then asks that his soul may burn up in hell as this paper is burning if he is not telling the truth. But neither of these oaths seems to tie the Chinaman down strictly to the truth. When you wish to be pretty certain that a Chinaman is coming very nearly to telling the truth, you insist that he be sworn by cutting off a chicken's head. What manner of oath is required by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We use
them all.
The chicken's head oath might be tried on members who ask too many questions!
I am not joking at all.

I understand there is some sort of international agreement between Great Britain and Japan. Would the minister consent to bringing that down so that we may have an opportunity of perusing it? I understand that the agreement allows certain concessions to Japan, and I should like to know what are the special considerations in regard to that country. I understand that it is not on account of any arrangement that we
make, but on account of an arrangement made between the Mother Country and the Japanese Empire.
Mr: MACKENZIE KING: With respect to the arrangement with Japan, it was arrived at by a representative of this country in conference with Japanese representatives, but I think the formal signatures were by ministers of the Departments of Foreign Affairs. The negotiation of the agreement, however, was entirely in the hands of the Honourable the Speaker of this House in conference with the Foreign Office of Japan. The agreement has been considered a secret agreement, and I doubt very much if the government could undertake to bring down the agreement without altering the understanding between the two governments. The understanding was that it would be kept secret. I might further say that negotiations have been continued within the last year and this year between the Japanese government and our own with a view of modifying the terms of that agreement. These negotiations are not yet finally consummated, and until they are,, it would be inadvisable to make any public statement regarding them.

I have every confidence in my right hon. leader, but I should like to know what can be brought down for public guidance in the matter. I am not asking for any confidential information at all, but can we have what has been reduced in writing and has been signed, and what is permitted to be made public.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think that
is all printed in the form of a state paper.
There is no particular secret about that. If my hon. friend wants the information I can give it to him.
I wish you would.

The Japanese Consul General was kind enough to send me a memorandum of the Japanese views, and I suppose copies have been sent to other members of the House. In that memorandum the details of this alleged gentlemen's agreement are set out. It is stated in the memorandum that the arrangement was to the effect that no more than four hundred Japanese labourers should be admitted in any one year. That is the effect of the famous Lemieux agreement as set out in the memorandum.
Supply-Immigration
Four hundred coming direct from Japan, was it not?
Yes.
It did not cover Japanese coming from other countries.

There is no secret
about it. I do not see why we should have any secret arrangements of this kind. Surely if we are going to have an agreement with any foreign government as to the number of its citizens that should be admitted to Canada the public are entitled to know what the agreement is. I personally am very much opposed to that kind of secret agreement. I am opposed in the first place, to the agreement itself, and I am opposed also to any secrecy regarding it. There should not be any secrecy about it. We have received the memorandum from the Japanese Consul General as to what the arrangement is with Japan, and further, while the matter is still secret here so far as the minister is concerned, we have received a statement from the Chinese Consul General as to the treaty with China. They do not seem to treat these matters as secret, and I do not see why there should be so much secrecy on the part of this government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With regard to what my hon. friend has said about secrecy, probably the best answer to that are the figures themselves. Our government has kept a record year by year of the number of Japanese that have come into the country for the last fifteen or twenty years. These figures are all published, and I think for the last ten years or more they will show that the number of Japanese labourers entering in one year was under four hundred, with the possible exception of one year.
In regard to what my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has said as to the agreement not applying to Japanese coming from other countries than Japan,
4 p.m. my impression is, and I think I am right in it, that our government will not permit any Japanese to enter unless he comes with a passport from Japan, signed by the Japanese Foreign Office. These passports are not given to Japanese who come other than direct from Japan, so under the present arrangement the Japanese of the restricted class who does not come direct from Japan is excluded.

But the trouble is this. It may be quite true, as the Prime Minister says, that the Japanese government officially

has kept the terms of this agreement, but the Japanese people themselves have not done so. I think the Minister of Immigration will agree with me when I make the statement that more Japanese have come into this country illegally than have come in legally.
I asked the minister just a moment ago what . precautions had been taken to prevent illegal entry of Chinese, and that would apply equally well to Japanese. I was thinking of the case that occurred the other day in Vancouver. A Japanese freighter came in with twenty-nine Japanese stowaways on board. The reason we heard anything about that was that the crew of the Japanese freighter had mutinied and taken possession of the ship, and the captain had wirelessed to the police at Vancouver to meet the boat. When she arrived at Vancouver the captain of the ship said that there were eighteen Japanese stowaways on board. The police endeavoured to locate them, and after a great deal of difficulty eventually found not eighteen, but twenty-nine Japanese in the coal bunkers. There you have the case of a Japanese freighter that is not supposed to carry passengers at all bringing in twenty-nine Japanese. If the crew had not mutinied, no doubt these men would have come into the country and later on have become citizens.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is one point that I think in all fairness my hon. friend ought to state in regard to this situation. The Canadian authorities, if I am rightly informed, were told about these Japanese in virtue of a wireless that was sent by the captain of the ship, who was himself a Japanese. It was the Japanese that brought the matter to the attention of the authorities in this country.

That was after the mutiny. According to the press despatches, these Japanese stowaways stated that they had come on board ship under an arrangement with certain people in Japan, that they had paid for the? privilege of coming to Canada, and they complained bitterly of their treatment in this country, and of the fact that they were not allowed to land. There is no doubt in the world that that has been going on for years, and that incident illustrates what has been happening, and explains why we have so many Japanese in this country;

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The point I wish to make is that what my hon. friend says in regard to Japanese coming in surreptitiously does not affect the agreement, or in

Supply-Immigration
any way what is accomplished or prevented under the agreement. That would take place, I assume, regardless of any arrangement. All I want to have clearly understood is that, as far as the agreement itself is concerned, the government has every reason to believe that the Japanese government has lived faithfully up to its letter. The agreement has been carried out in good faith by both parties.
But if this kind of thing is allowed to go on, should not the Japanese-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that no Japanese ship shall be allowed to land in Canada.

No that is not what I am arguing. The Prime Minister has said that the Japanese have carried out the gentlemen's agreement and lived up to it ever since it was entered into. The important point is that the Japanese government is not preventing Japanese leaving Japan to come to Canada.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING' Does the hon. member mean to say that the Japanese government is responsible for the Japanese who came in surreptitiously?
I say they are not taking any precautions to stop the emigration of Japanese citizens to Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am informed exactly the opposite-that they are doing all in their power to see that the agreement is lived up to. Cases may arise which are beyond the control of the government. Japanese may come in surreptitiously. That is beyond the control of the Japanese government. I think it is due to the government of Japan to say that it has been made very clear, so far as this government is concerned, that the government of Japan is doing its utmost to keep faith in the matter of the agreement. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) who is present, and who had to do with immigration previously, will agree with what I say, that during his term of office he had every reason to believe that the Japanese government were living up to the agreement in good faith.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was never in charge of immigration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But the right hon. member was Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, but never in charge of immigration. That was a separate matter and I was not in charge of that. Under
the terms of that contract, each government undertook to limit immigration to Canada. Did the contract by the Japanese government say that not more than so many-referred to yesterday as 400-Japanese labourers should land in Canada? Was that a covenant on the part of the Japanese government? Or does the contract read in this way, that Canada is justified in preventing more than 400 Japanese landing in this country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I might answer by saying that the first agreement that was made was in the nature of a treaty in regard to trade matters between Japan and Great Britain, to which this country became a party. One of the terms of that treaty, to which this parliament was a party or of which it approved, was that the subjects of Japan were to have free entrance into Canada. The treaty guaranteed-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the Anglo-Japan-ese treaty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. Full right was given to the Japanese to 'come into this country under that treaty. It is open to parliament, if its members so desire, to denounce that treaty, to cease to be a party to it, and to lose the benefit to this country in trade matters which the treaty has helped us to secure. That conceivably might be the effect of eliminating the clause giving to the Japanese as citizens of Japan the right to come freely into this country. It was pointed out at the time that this right of entry would not be satisfactory to the people of Canada, that possibly the treaty might have to be denounced if that right was to be maintained. The Japanese government offered itself to restrict the number of persons coming into the country in accordance with arrangements which might be made between the government of Canada.^nd' the government of Japan. It was a matter, I think, mostly of national pride with the Japanese. They desired to preserve, in the face of the world at all events, the right of their citizens to go anywhere, and I say quite frankly to hon. gentlemen opposite that if this- parliament, and particularly our friends from British Columbia, prefer to end any agreement, so far as trade is concerned, between Japan and Canada, which may affect immigration, they have only to say so, they have only to insist that such rights as are secured by treaty shall be ended, and we can very soon settle in that way, if that way will settle it, the whole question of Japanese im- -migration to Canada. If, on the other hand, this country wishes to preserve trade with the Orient, we shall have to have some regard
Supply-Immigration

for matters which with respect to their citizens the governments of the Orient regard as all important. If the government of Japan is agreeable to making an arrangement with this country which will preserve to the government of Japan such rights as it regards as essential to its citizens, and at the same time avoid as effectively as any other method possibly can, the immigration of labour from Japan to this country, I think it will be infinitely better for all to adopt the latter course.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I now wish to say a word of two on the matter of the covenants of the government. I want to say that while in office it was never represented to me, nor have I any reason to say now, that the Japanese government have not complied with, or endeavoured faithfully to comply with, the covenant. I never saw the terms of it, and never had occasion to review the terms, but if the terms are such as the Prime Minister states, that the Japanese government undertook to prevent more than 400 coming to this country, and then if more than 400 come, it means the government has not complied with the treaty, although Japan may have endeavoured to comply with it. It may be that in regard to a binding contract with Japan, that country has found itself unable to comply with it. If that is the case, is not the government in a position to charge against the 400, or whatever the number is, any number that come in surreptitiously or in any way whatever? So that no more than 400 can come in, and no more will be allowed to enter, no matter how they come in.
The other matter is before the House today but I do not subscribe to the belief for a minute that we must abandon all trade with Japan, if we assert control over our own immigration and assert it to whatever extent we desire. The matter of trade is not a one-sided matter. It is a matter that is important to Canada and important to Japan. The Japanese are just as wise as we are. The Japanese control their immigration and we can control ours, and I am one of those who believe that we can control it just as absolutely as we desire, and whatever the consequences may be, they will not be any more disastrous to us than to the other country. In a word, they will not come in.

I think if the Premier is alluding to the trade treaty of 1913, he will recall that in that treaty, which was ratified by Canada there was this stipulation:
This treaty shall be subject to all the terms of the Immigration Act.
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]
A division of opinion has arisen since then, as to whether the words "Immigration Act" in that treaty refer to the immigration act of that day or also cover any immigration act that might be subsequently passed, but it is abundantly plain that it did cover the im-migation act of that day.
Now that trade treaty between Japan and Canada was made or passed in 1913, and the revised or consolidated Immigration Act of 1912 contained provisions dating back some years, which gives the Minister of Immigration absolute power to exclude Asiatics under a general provision, something like that in the bill I endeavoured to bring down the other day. It says:
The Minister of Immigration can reject the nationals of a people or a race whose national conditions-
Or some words to that effect.
-and whose habits and whose climatic conditions r where they come from, render them unsuitable to assimilate with the people of Canada.
The provision is quite broad, and under it, in the year 1912, or prior to that, the Minister of Immigration had that power. Then, this trade treaty of 1913 undoubtedly reserved the provisions of that Immigration Act, so that, 1 submit, it will be possible to do away with the gentlemen's agreement to-day and totally to exclude Japanese or other Asiatics under the provisions of the Immigration Act as it was subsequently reenacted more forcibly, without interfering with the right and privilege of trading with Japan. Trading with Japan is a matter in which we are vitally interested, and it is of as vital interest to Japan as it is to us. But under the terms of the provision which I have mentioned, it is not necessary to do away with the trade treaty if we wish to do away with the gentlemen's agreement.
Another matter in connection with the gentlemen's agreement has not been mentioned in this House. In addition to the 400 who are allowed into Canada every year, there is also what is called some land settlement scheme by which every Japanese owning a hundred acres of land can bring in ten Japs. Apparently, however, there is no restriction as to time; if he has 100 acres of land, he can bring in ten Japs to-day and ten next month. There is no provision as to how often he can bring in those ten Japs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Under what?
Under the gentlemen's agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman is misinformed as to that. Any

Supply-Immigration
restriction as to numbers of labourers coming in will apply to such labourers as may be brought in for the very purpose to which he refers.

It may be that I am unable to read the gentlemen's agreement correctly, for I must say that the gentlemen's agreement, as I have seen it, is one of the most abstruse documents 1 have ever put my eyes on, and I may have interpreted it incorrectly. According to my understanding, the number was limited to 400 labourers per annum, plus the number allowed in as labourers on Jap farms. I will, however, accept the Prime Minister's interpretation.
Another thing that we might well notice under the gentlemen's agreement in connection with this matter is this, and it actually occurred three years ago. The Minister of Immigration in times of unusual unemployment has the power-and he exercised it three years ago-to prohibit any immigration into Canada of British subjects whatever, of unskilled or skilled labour, and he did so exercise that power. But he was unable under this gentlemen's agreement to prohibit the entry of those 400 Japanese. Thus, we had the wonderful situation of these orientals coming in at the rate of 400 a year, whereas, owing to unusual labour conditions in this country, our own British subjects were unable to enter Canada.
As regards the shipment of Japanese to which the hon. member for New Westminister (Mr. McQuarrie) referred, I think he stated the case correctly; but he omitted one feature of it as it was worked out in the press. It is much more difficult, I might say in passing, to prohibit the entry of Japanese than Chinamen. The Chinese come in our own Canadian Pacific boats, owned and manned by white men and these boats tie up at our wharf. The immigration officers visit and search the ship and keep a watchman on the wharf, whilst the ship is in port, so that it is practically very difficult for Chinamen to enter in that way illegally. But the Jap has his own line of steamships with not one white man on board. He pulls into the wharf and goes through the customs inspection. Then there is only a guard on the wharf at night, perhaps a sleepy old man, walking up and down. What is to prevent, with the full connivance of the officers, all of whom are Japanese, a boat or a launch coming on the other side of the ship, away from this sleepy watchman and taking off a small or moderate number, for a Jap never overplays his hand; he will only bring in twenty or thirty every ship-load.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: How would an exclusion law prevent that sort of thing?

I will come to that in a
minute. I suggest that that is a way in which they are put ashore, and in some measure that accounts for the extraordinary difference between the number of those coming in legally and those who are now here. As regards this particular case, it would appear that these 29 stowaways had paid a sum of money to be taken over to Canada, and on the way over, through some misapprehension or misunderstanding, they found they were going, not as they thought, to San Francisco, for which they had apparently paid their good money, but to Vancouver. It was not altogether a mutiny of the crew that took place; it was a mutiny of those stowaways, backed by some of the crew. They swarmed up on board and practically took possession of the ship, saying: "We will not go to Vancouver; we will sail to where we paid our money to go," and it was that that led the captain of the boat to wireless in for assistance when he came into the harbour. The boat did not pull into the wharf; it anchored out in the harbour. The police came aboard and arrested, I think, one or two of the crew. There were no stowaways visible; but as soon as the police boat went away-there were just one or two immigration officers in it,- those stowaways came up again, and they compelled that boat to get up steam and come into the wharf. They appeared to be ignorant of the fact that there was a wireless apparatus aboard or how it was used, and the captain again sent a wireless message for assistance. When the boat docked, a swarm of policemen rushed aboard and arrested those who were making the trouble. Then they began to look for the Japanese stowaways, and they could not find any. The hon. member for New Westminister said that they were in the coal bunkers. That apparently would be a simple place to find them. The men found that apparently there was nothing but coal in the bunkers, and they could not get at the stowaways without removing three or four hundred_tons of coal. They knew that the men were there, but they did not know how to get at them. Some man, with more than usual ingenuity- and the minister should promote him-conceived the idea of boring holes through the deck; they put down long rods until they came to a place where, there was no coal, and presently they came to what apparently was Asiatic flesh. The Japs were lying in a heap in a concealed chamber in the coal, and they removed enough coal to get at them. This

Supply-Immigration
was a cunningly concealed place that the average man would not find at all. This was not done, and could not be done, without the full knowledge and consent of the Japanese line of boats. I have no doubt the Japanese government kept its agreement; but these are the nationals, and this is the way in which they act. As the hon. member for New Westminster says, had it not been for this untoward incident of their being scheduled to the wrong port, nothing would have been heard about the matter. That goes on, more or less, all the time.
To come to the Prime Minister's query as to how this can be prevented, I would say that a total exclusion act would not prevent that in any degree whatever; it would still go on. The remedy is to have a measure of exclusion, coupled with what, I think, the minister provides for as regards Chinamen to some extent, namely, a system of registration. When Mr. Jap or Mr. Chinaman-this is the case at present as regards Chinamen- comes in, he has a registration certificate given him, practically as we had in the war. In years to come, when any of those men get into trouble or travel, they can be asked by an official to produce their registration cards, and if they cannot produce them or give some explanation of their loss or so on, then they are liable to deportation. That is the case under the new act as regards Chinamen, and that is the remedy for evasions of the act.
I made it my business to have a talk with some of the prominent officials of the Department of Immigration as regards Chinamen. What they told me was this, that there was no definition, no rule, no formula, yet devised by their department-and they had been very strenuous in the matter-which had yet worked successfully, because the minute the Chinamen understood the rule, they sat down and evaded it. They told me how they evaded the rule in regard to Chinamen coming in as sons. Men who had not been out of Canada for thirty years would bring in boys of eighteen as their sons. The way the thing was worked was this. These would have to be the sons of a* merchant. What was a merchant? A merchant was one actively engaged in some city of Canada with a certain sum invested. They got up bogus companies. Supposing I am a Chinese parent, and working at tailoring in Montreal, for some of this occurred in Montreal. I go down to a regular firm which makes a business of this. Supposing this is a firm of exporters or importers; I put S500 cash into the business; I get a job there as porter or some
[Mr. Neill.)
job I am fitted for, for a month or two. I then claim that the boy coming in is my son, and the immigration officials, who appear to have been very zealous on the job, make inquiries and even send a man down to ascertain whether I am really working there busy. Thej'' find that I am at work and they look up the books and discover that everything is straight, and that as a matter of fact I did put $500 into the business. After a great deal of consideration they may grant my claim or they may not; and when they go back to the same firm a month afterwards and inquire about another man they find that I have taken my $500 out of the business and gone back to my tailoring or laundering in the next street. Now, these are not hypothetical cases; they are actual occurrences as these officials told them to me.
As regards the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. McQuarrie) that we should be cautious in defining a merchant-I believe he said we should be very definite-I may inform the committee that the officials of the department are of the opinion that we should leave this matter to their discretion, and I am inclined to support them in this view. So that instead of having a clear-cut definition of what constitutes a merchant, it is my opinion that it should be left as flexible as possible and within the judgment of the officials; because the moment you make the definition rigid these people will find some way of getting round it. On the other hand, if you made the definition broad, and left some room for the exercise of judgment on the part of the officials, they would be in a better position to see that the provision was not evaded. Last year eight merchants came in under that category, and my informant told me of a case where a merchant wanted to bring a boy in who was really his son. He was a wealthy man in the ladies' tailoring business out West, but they refused to let this immigrant in because they claimed that the father was not a merchant according to their interpretation of the act. The Chinaman asked them what they considered a merchant to be, and they replied, "We regard as a merchant only anyone who is dealing in Chinese goods, importing or exporting direct, and carrying on a traffic with China." So that this man, although he has two or three stores and is wealthy, could not prove that he was a merchant and his son was rejected. For that reason therefore it is advisable not to define too strictly the term "merchant". The hon. member suggested that we should exclude merchants; not, I suggest, however, if the matter is left in that broad way; because I

Supply-Immigration
tliink we do want to do trade with China and Japan, and so long as they are genuine bona fide merchants trading with the East I do not think there can be any objection to them.

In the previous part of the discussion something was said about Chinese children coming into the country, and I might make a further statement in regard to Japanese. Not only do the Japanese bring their children in, but in some cases they furnish them with Canadian naturalization papers as soon as they land. That may ap-. pear to be a rash statement, but it is one that I can prove, because at one of the sittings of the British Columbia Fisheries Commission last year we had a witness who was the assistant secretary of the Japanese Fisheries Association of No. 2 District. I believe he gave evidence at Port Essington. That gentleman appeared before us and spoke English very well. He was well educated, and we found that he had attended the Columbian College in New Westminster. I asked him whether he was naturalized and he said he was. I inquired as to when he had got naturalized and ascertained that at the time of his naturalization he was eight years of age. I believe he was twenty-two when he gave evidence. I asked him how he had managed to get naturalization when only eight years of age and he replied, "My father arranged that for me." I asked him when that had been done and he said it had been arranged the year his father brought him from Japan. That evidence was given before the Fisheries Commission on oath, and of course it is available to any hon. gentleman who cares to see it.
I might refer to the last remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in reference to the trade treaty. The right hon. gentleman said that if the members from British Columbia so desired that treaty could be abrogated, and he seemed to hold this out as somewhat of a threat to' us. Now, my stand in regard to that treaty was made plain when I submitted my resolution in regard to the exclusion of oriental immigrants, and one of the things I sugested was that this government should request the Imperial government to give notice of the abrogation of the treaty so far as Canada was concerned. I am not afraid of" the loss of trade at all; I am not afraid that the Japanese will not do business with us if we keep them out of this country. The Japanese is a man who does business along business lines and buys his goods where it profits him most to buy them. He will buy our goods just so long as he thinks he is getting value for his money, and
when he realizes that he is not he will deal with someone else. If he does not come to us for the goods which he at present gets from us, where is he going to get them? He is not going to go to the United States, because the same reasons would apply there as apply in this country to the Japanese. The United States certainly does not wish the Japanese to go there, so where will he go to get the goods he receives from us? This trade treaty is a trade bogey and I am not at all afraid of it. So far as this particular member from British Columbia is concerned you can abrogate the treaty right away.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let me make it clear to my hon. friend that I was not attempting to utter any threats; nothing would be further from my mind than to do anything of that kind. I merely desired to inform the House of the possible consequences that might ensue from certain acts as represented to me.

There is something else of significance I would draw to the attention of the committee in connection with this treaty. It is provided that the citizens of Japan shall not be discriminated against in any way in this country. That has led to a restriction of the rights of the legislatures of the provinces. It is well known that in British Columbia we have from year to year, I do not know on how many different occasions, passed legislation which might be said to come within this class, and all that legislation has been disallowed as discriminating against the Japanese. We had an example of this last year when the British Columbia government passed an order in council providing that no orientals should be employed on timber lands leased from the Crown in the right of the province. Afterwards an act was passed validating that order in council, and the order in council and the act having been taken before the courts of our province, and the Supreme Court of Canada those courts held them to be invalid as conflicting with the Japanese treaty. What did this government do? I must take exception to the course that was followed on that occasion. This government disallowed the provincial enactment. It seems to me that that disallowance was unnecessary if the courts were right. But this government went out of its way to disallow that provincial enactment, as Liberal governments had been doing on a great many occasions. It seemed to be the policy of Conservative governments in British Columbia to pass legislation along these lines and of Liberal governments to disallow it. Anyway, this government went
Supply-Immigration

out of its way to disallow this provincial enactment. British Columbia took the case to the Privy Council, and the Privy Council, as I am advised by the press despatches, has held that the province was right in passing the act. So that this government disallowed an act which the government of British Columbia had a perfect right to pass.
I would like to ask the minister what investigation has been made in regard to the incident of the Japanese freighter? If the Japanese government are sincere they will investigate the matter over there, and if the statements made by the stowaways are correct they should be able to put their finger on the gang who are carrying on this illegitimate business. Here is something that should be investigated, and I would like to know what has been done in the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I may say that after that occurrence the Japanese consul called upon me of his own volition and referred to the matter. He intimated that the Japanese government were having it looked into.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Joliffe has gone to investigate, but we have not had a report from him up to the moment.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Exhibitions-salaries and expenses, $140,000.
What exhibitions is this money for, and is it the intention that Canada shall participate in the Empire exhibition to be held in 1924?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is our intention to participate in that event. Mr. Tolmie has just returned from the Old Country, but we have not yet had a report from him. For the collection of exhibits we have an appropriation of $35,000. For exhibitions in Great Britain and the United States the amount appropriated is $70,000 and for permanent exhibitions in those countries another $8,000 is provided. The appropriations for exhibitions are heavier this year on account of the advertising, which we are extending; we hope to increase our participation in exhibitions because of the resulting advantage to Canada in the way of advertising. We have been represented at Tampa last year and this year, at considerable expense, but we think it pays thus to display our products.

I would like to point out the necessity of making a showing in those countries from which we hope to get immigrants. When I was in England I attended the big Royal Show, and I found that the Canadian exhibit there was not nearly equal to that of South Africa. South African pro-

ducts and the capabilities of that country were all well represented and their comer was crowded, while Canada's exhibit attracted very little attention. I have no doubt the minister was trying to economize, but it struck me as a very poor kind of economy. If any important effect is to be produced we must make a showing at least as good as that put up by other countries.
How much does it cost to collect exhibits for the purposes of these exhibitions? How many men are employed? What are their names, and are they employed the year round?

I have not the names of the persons employed, or the number. The item of $35,000 is to cover the 'purchase price of samples of grains, grasses, fruits, vegetables and mineral specimens, together with the expenses of the field men.
I understand that these are special Canadian exhibits made at state fairs. What kind of exhibits are shown-natural products, manufactured articles, food stuffs, or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not seen any of these exhibitions, but I get very glowing reports confcerning them. For example, I have a letter from the Exhibition Association at Tampa asking that our space there be doubled. I do not think, however, that it would be wise to do that, because the cost would be considerable; I would rather try to cover a larger area and enable more people to see the exhibits. We are trying to attract agricultural people to our country; therefore our exhibits are largely of agricultural products.

They are
under the supervision of some government official?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, of Mr. Tolmie.

I got a report from a person whom I can vouch for that there was an official in Winnipeg-I do not know whether he was employed temporarily or permanently-gathering samples of grain at the end of July. We all realize that in western Canada you cannot at that time of the year collect samples of grain that will be of any value for exhibition purposes. I see no reason why money should be wasted in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did see one of our exhibits at Chicago, and one of the difficulties experienced there resulted from a lack of the exercise of due care in

Supply-Immigration
the selection of the samples of wheat in head, with the result that it was over ripe. I do know that a Mr. Smith was temporarily employed on this work last year. I will, however, get the names for my hon. friend of all who were employed and the period at which they did their work.

The minister will agree that the end of July is no time to collect samples of grain in the West. As I have said, I see no reason why money should be spent in a futile search of that kind. I have no objection to representatives of the department collecting the samples at the proper time, but it cannot be done at the end of July.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not seen the samples received this year and I cannot say where they came from, but I understand that Mr. Tolmie is highly pleased with them. The getting of good samples this year was not a difficult matter, owing to the extra good crop that was grown in western Canada, particularly in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

I happen to know something with regard to the gathering of these samples in Manitoba. The work is done by one of the permanent employees of the Immigration department there; as I understand it, it is part of his regular duties. As to going out in July, I may say that part of his work is to gather samples of native and cultivated grasses, and that of course, has to be done in July.
What was the total expenditure under this vote last year, and what was the proportion spent in each country where there was an exhibition?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
For the
eleven months of the last year the total expenditure was $121,998. That includes $12,000 in connection with the visit of Colonel Belcher to Canada on behalf of the British Empire Exhibition.
We have not the answer yet. We spent last year $121,000. In what different countries was the money spent, and in what proportions?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the figures here, but I will get them for my hon. friend.

We started out with this item in 1921-22 in the amount of $90,000; last year it was $115,000, and the appropriation this year is $140,000. Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting to make a few remarks with regard to immigration. I restrained myself last night because I thought the minister was anxious to pass the item we were then discussing, and also because my remarks might have been out of order like those of a good many other members who spoke yesterday. I never like to speak very long, so I am glad to see the clock says twenty minutes to six. I intend to close within twenty minutes.
I think it is my duty at the outset to express my views on immigration in order to offset some of the views presented by members from western Canada, especially from the prairie provinces. My sympathies are with the acting-Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart). I think it is evident from the amount of information that he could not give us today that he is overworked and is not able to keep in touch with every branch of his department. Therefore I would very strongly recommend that the government appoint a minister to take sole charge of immigration, which is one of the most important questions we have to deal with. My sympathy for the minister is also aroused because of certain statements that have been made from his own side of the House as well as from this side.
I wish to express my appreciation of my honoured leader from Brandon (Mr. Forke) on his stand in regard to immigration. Wherever he has spoken in the Dominion he has said that what we wanted were more people of the right type, and I agree with him. I also wish to congratulate the member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) on his contribution to the debate, although he had the temerity to say that probably some of us farmers in Manitoba tried to scratch too much land. However, I quite agree that this is so in many cases. In fact I have myself tried to scratch too much land.
I am glad, Mr. Chairman, that no member from the province of Manitoba defamed his province. I think it is a credit to my colleagues from Manitoba. We know we have hard conditions in western Canada; indeed, there is not a member of this House outside the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Jelliff) more hard up than myself.

How do you
know?

And if the resolution of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) had carried I would have been even more hard up. But here let me make a statement of a personal character. I left the province of Quebec forty-one years ago next month.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You were brought up in a good province.

I left as a baby and have lived in the province of Manitoba on the banks of the Red river since 1882. I have travelled throughout the whole of western Canada right to the coast and know it about as well as the average man in this country. And I might state right here that one of the biggest troubles in this House is that we do not know our own country sufficiently well. I want to extend an invitation to hon. members from eastern Canada to come out to the West and see our country.
The climate is too dry.

I may tell the hon. member for Quebec South that we are going to have a vote on that question in Manitoba next June. So you see that I have a fair knowledge of the province of Manitoba, and to that province I wish chiefly to refer. No one has more faith in western Canada than I have; no one has more faith in Manitoba than I have. We are hard up, but we are hopeful. In Manitoba we have more and better land prepared than has been the case at any other time in the history of the province. This question of immigration is a peculiar one in some respects. Mr. C. H. Burnell, president of the United Farmers of Manitoba, stated that the question of immigration came down to this: do we want neighbours? We want them in Manitoba. Do we want more children to fill our schools? We do want them. Do we want more people to patronize our railways? We do. If my hon. friends in Alberta do not want immigrants, I may tell the minister that he may send to Manitoba those he has allotted to Alberta, and we will give them a good welcome.
I would like to point out also that through a short-sighted policy-at least I think so; I may be wrong-on the part of our late provincial government, the Mennonites are leaving the province and going to Mexico. I have great respect for them; they are good farmers. They are leaving some of the best lands we have in Manitoba, and to-day those lands, with buildings in good condition, can

be had at reasonable prices. So that there is quite an advantage available to people who come to our part of the country. I would advise the minister, however, to endeavour to get men who have a little capital, because to have money is a great advantage and to be without it is a serious handicap. The question arises, where are we going to get immigrants? I suggest that if the minister devoted all his energy to getting back the Canadians who have gone from our country to the United States, he would be doing something well worth while. There are millions of Canadians over there whose hearts are still with Canada. If the minister would endeavour to bring back a lot of the French Canadians, those families where the stork comes round about once a year, he would not have to give his attention to child immigration from older countries. And there are not only French Canadians; there are good Scotch Canadians in those eastern states-and I know how good the Scotch are, because I have a Scotch wife. Then there are the Irish Canadians-and I am standing beside an Irishman right here. These are the people we should try to bring into the country, people who have a certain amount of money. I am not in favour of going to Europe to get immigrants. I have nothing against the European people; I think a lot of them. But under present conditions in Europe you cannot get immigrants from there who have any money and it is going to be hard for anyone who comes here without it. I know from conversations I have had and from inquiries I have received that there are many people in the eastern states that are willing to come to Canada and assume their share in the task of building up our country. I would, therefore, strongly advise the minister to use his best efforts to get immigrants from there.
Under this item of $600,000 I do not know exactly what the proposal of the minister is. but it seems to me that it is going to be more or less in the nature of assistance to steamship companies. I may be wrong, and I hope I am. But I do think that'if that $600,000 were used to carry on a propaganda in the United States with a view to bringing back our own good Canadians the result would be more beneficial than any payments out for steamship fares. In Manitoba, within a comparatively short distance of the city of Winnipeg, we have all kinds of wheat lands that are unoccupied and that can be bought at a small sum per acre. If you bring immigrants to Manitoba you do not immediately have to start to build branch line railways; they are there already and those who come

Private Bills
to our province can all settle within a reasonable distance of railway facilities, which is no small advantage for any immigrant. Then Manitoba being the oldest province in the West, we have far more institutions than they have in the other provinces; in fact, as the member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) quite correctly said the other day, we are over-institutionalized. I think the minister should certainly do all he can to give Manitoba a large share of immigrants.
I stated, Sir, that I wished to conclude my remarks within twenty minutes, and I shall not detain the committee longer. But I did not want to let this debate go by without expressing my views on the questions before the committee and without expressing my faith in Canada. I am Canadian born and I am proud of it. I repeat that no one has more faith in this country than I have and, at the same time, less money in his pocket.

On section 1-Change of name and rights saved.	,
I would like some explanation of the meaning of this bill.

I have not charge of the bill but I am familiar with it. I think the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is very familiar with this subject. It is merely a company which looks after the collection and dissemination of newspaper news. They are changing their name, and turning the company from an ordinary share company to a company which will have no stock issue at all. The different newspapers will have a representative in that company. Those representatives are called shareholders, although as a matter of fact they will have no money in it. The management will look after the collection and distribution of news particularly for the newspapers interested in it. They change from a share company into one without money shares and one that is to be without profit.
Is it not pretty much a mohopoly in regard to news items? Will the bringing of this company under Dominion legislation have any effect in regard to any person suing the company?
There is a provision in the bill reserving all rights in that regard. As to monopolies, I think my hon. friend is looking after all monopolies this year, even in the newspapers.
Is there anything in the bill to prevent any newspaper that may be subsequently established from going into the association?
I do not think so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I might say, in the absence of the hon. member in charge of the bill, that this measure has two purposes. One is that the word "limited" now existing shall be dropped. The company is now known as the Canadian Press Limited and the word "limited" will be dropped. The purpose of the bill is to convert the company from one with share capital to a corporation without share capital and with no participation in profits by anyone, and there is a clause in the bill which provides that if there is any money made it cannot be distributed as dividends.

I am glad that the Minister of Finance is in his seat at the present time. I just want to make a general observation as to the estimates, about something which I have always felt was wrong. My hon. friend knows how hard it is to get things changed. I want to draw not only the attention of this House but his attention in particular to this matter.
One of the great defects in our method of book-keeping and the presentation of our estimates at the present time is that no one can very well find out what the cost of anything is to the country. Just to illustrate. Civil government is supposed to carry the salary lists of the country. It is supposed to have segregated there the salaries having regard to the different activities of the country, but it does not by any manner of means include them all. We have a way of putting in salaries here, and there, and the other place. We have a switch of salaries this year from one vote to another vote. I am not saying it is wrong, except that the whole principle is absolutely wrong, because by doing that any method of comparison disappears. There ought to be one account for the salaries. Take, for example, the Department of Immigration and Colonization. We have in the first instance a civil government list amounting to $272,000. That is all salaries. Then in vote No. 52 we have for the outside service, salaries amounting to $700,000, which has to be added to the other salaries. It really would be a good thing if everybody short of the expert could know just what the different activities of the country were costing to the country. My hon. friend (Mr. Forke) asked for a more detailed statement of this item. I can quite appreciate his request for information on the large amount that will come up for consideration
next week, but I want to point out that this will be a very difficult matter to itemize We are endeavouring at the moment to make an arrangement with the Overseas Settlement Board for co-operation. If we do not get co-operation we cannot spend the money. I explained the proposal the other day, and I will explain it again to-night briefly. The first idea we had was the bringing of children from the Old Country. I pointed out that there was a place for these children in Canada, but that they would not be brought here if there were no foster homes for them. I have a list of the homes or places from where these children will be secured in Great Britain, and I though it was good business to ask for an appropriation to encourage the immigration of these young people. The organizations that have been doing this work have found it exceedingly difficult in recent years to secure the funds for the maintenance of the homes and carrying on the work of the education of these children and the training and clothing of them. It has been carried on very largely by voluntary effort on the part of English people, and there is a number of very admirable homes from which these children can be selected. I sent Mr. Smart over there to make an examination of the children, first to see where we could secure the kind of children that would be desirable to bring to Canada, because I want to assure the committee that we do not desire to bring any children who would be undesirable. They will all be carefully selected and brought to Canada on application from Canadian people themselves. Unless there are homes for them they will not be brought. It has to be borne in mind that we expect the Empire Settlement Board to join us and put up the same amount of money we will put up, and in this particular case we do not expect any return. It will be a straight grant. I had estimated-I do not know whether the amount will cover the cost -$80 per head to pay the passage of these children; that would be $40 for the Canadian government and $40 for the Overseas Settlement Board. I will read you the names of the homes. There are many other homes in addition to these where fine children can be procured, but these are homes that have been in existence for a number of years, and eventually I hope that, perhaps,, we can branch out, if this scheme proves successful, and there is a demand for children, or a place for them to go. These homes will be inspected as well as the children, so that the complaint that is so frequently made that children are being made slaves and are not receiving attention will be avoided as far as possible. It would

Thus, this does not involve the expenditure of a huge sum of money for administration, it involves two of our officials in the Old Land making selections, and I notice that a little difficulty has arisen in connection with this very question in the joint action of the Australian government and the British government. I want to assure the committee that if they allow me to have this money, the most careful selection will be made of those children who will be brought to Canada, and also, of other people who are coming. I know I am being criticized very frequently because we are somewhat anxious to maintain the standards; that is, we want those who come to Canada to be mentally, morally and physically fit. I think that is desirable; I have always felt so. More than that, I think these children will assimilate into the life of Canada, will be assimilated into Canadian

homes, will become Canadian citizens and will, perhaps, in a much better way adapt themselves to Canadian conditions than those who are of more mature years' before coming to Canada. We have no definite arrangement at the moment with the Imperial authorities, because some considerable discussion is involved as to what methods are to be employed. A day or two ago, I received a wire intimating that the British authorities were viewing our proposal with favour.
Will the minister kindly answer my question as regards the minimum age of the child?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We propose to bring the bulk of the children between the ages of eight and fourteen. I know there is a great difference of opinion as to what age the child should be, but purely as an experiment, we propose to bring out at least a couple of hundred boys and girls between the ages of fourteen and seventeen, if we can secure places for them.

Will the same interest be shown in finding homes for the children? I speak from a humanitarian point of view. The reason I ask the question is that I have, in many instances, seen children placed in homes where they did not receive quite as good treatment as, in my opinion, they might have. Will the department see that the homes are real homes for these children?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have no complaint to offer as regards any province; but I think Ontario is, perhaps, the best field in which to test out a plan of this kind, and Quebec is similarly situated. Those provinces are more thickly populated, and they have classes of homes into which those children can, perhaps, be taken, and an environment that will give the children a better chance. I see the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) looking at me. I am now speaking of the older provinces.
Mr. CALDW'ELL: Is Quebec not more inclined to grow her own children?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was very much interested in looking over the figures to see that quite a number of those children go into Quebec, in spite of the fact that the people of that province, to their credit, raise a large number of very fine children. The older provinces are undoubtedly the best places in which to put those children. Their homes are established, and while the West will take some of, those children, in the main, they will go into the older pro-

Supply-Immigration
vinces. I am not so familiar with Quebec; but as regards Ontario, in discussing the matter with Mr. Manning Doherty, I found that they had not only agricultural agents but representatives travelling almost continually visitmg*those homes. In Ontario, they have and have had for years an officer in charge, whose business it is to be going about the country constantly visiting these homes. We propose on behalf of the federal government, if possible, to visit these children twice a year, and before a child is placed, to get a recommendation from the responsible people in the neighbourhood as to the character of the home into which the child is going. That is most essential. If you are careful about the selection of the child, it is just as, well to be careful as regards the home into which you put the child.
As regards the $40 which is the amount, I -think, the minister mentioned as Canada's obligation, the homes where those children are placed would not be obliged to return the $40?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, that is a grant outright.
Is it the minister's intention to spend this entire sum on child immigration?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, that covers only $200,000.

The minister has stressed the question of selection on the part of the department, and I am glad to know that he is not unmindful of the question of inspection. In days gone by, I have had a little to do with the Middlemore children who are the ones who have been brought to New Brunswick in recent years. I would advise the minister that, as far as possible, in each province where it is pi'oposed to place these children, he should have a permanent standing committee in each local community. For instance, in New Brunswick he might arrange -and I think this could be arranged through the authorities of the Middlemore Home-to have a committee in the shire town of every county. I am not unmindful of the fact that a man's neighbours do not usually give him a bad standing, especially in matters of this kind, and I have known of citizens applying for those children being given characters not altogether warranted. If you had a standing committee in each central community, I am sure you would find they would take the pains to sift the character of applicants, so as to make sure that those children were not being put into improper homes. I have known of cases where the most outrageous
cruelty has been committed against such children. That is a crime the country will not stand for; but it is better to prevent it than to cure it after. The minister read a list of the homes which have been sending children to Canada. I wonder if he has on his list a home known as the Cossar Home for boys. I would like to tell the minister about the activities of this home which is one of the smaller institutions of this kind. In the city of Glasgow there is a citizen known as Dr. George C. Cossar, who for a number of years past has been engaged in the work of rescuing the waifs of that city. At his own expense he takes them in and cares for them and sends them out to a large farm at Gagetown in the province of New Brunswick. The boys he sends out are for the most part around the ages mentioned by the minister. They are taught practical farming and are kept on the farm until they are ready to shift for themselves. This gentleman has brought out to this country at his own expense a very large number of boys, and in view of the fact that he is the only person engaged in work of this kind, what he has achieved is, I think, remarkable. The boys who have been settled in New Brunswick have with one single exception been a credit to him and to themselves, and when the war broke out, I am informed by the manager of the farm, every single one of them enlisted and fought for his country. The minister might tell us whether he intends to give any encouragement to agencies such as this one, which has done such a splendid work. If he would like to have more information privately I should be glad to give it to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think
that it is good business to begin this work only with such organizations as have made a success of it and can exercise Some care in the mattter of selection and in inspection afterwards. Our Mr. Smart, who has had a long experience in the work, will visit the children and make inquiries about the home. I quite realize the responsibility that we are taking upon ourselves in a matter of this kind, and if we make mistakes the advertising would be very bad for us. I think it is well for us, therefore, to begin with the people who have experience and who have made a success of this sort of work, because after all there are only certain classes of people who are adapted for engaging in work of this character. I assure the committee that we shall try to exercise the greatest care in whatever is done in this matter.
