The minister said something about selecting the children from good homes. Does he mean homes in the Old Land or in Canada as well, and are these children orphans?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Smart
reports, and I gather the same thing from Commissioner Lamb of the Salvation Army, that there are in Great Britain innumerable families of children who have no very bright outlook for the future and whose parents find it difficult to maintain them. These children are a splendid class of young people, and the parents would be willing, if they were assured that the children were going into homes under proper supervision, to allow them to come out on some engagement or other. But we are not attempting that, because I think the committee will readily understand how difficult it would be to have an organization that could take care of immigration of that sort. At any rate we are not attempting it at the moment. Later on we may branch out in this direction, but personally I want to go carefully and slowly in beginning an undertaking of this kind. After all, bringing children to Canada is not a new thing for the organizations I have mentioned. So far as that goes it would be merely a matter of giving them a per capita allowance for the children they brought out and established. We have done a considerable amount of this work in the past, not by way of per capita grants, but by means of a general grant. But if we are to undertake the thing in a systematic way we must accept some responsibility for the selection both of the children and of the home.

Is it the policy of the department in such cases to have the children legally adopted by the foster parents? If so, at the expiration of what time does the adoption take place? Further is any supervision maintained by the department in the case of adoption?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is a matter to which we have not given a great deal of consideration, deeming it wise to follow the procedure adopted by these well-organized institutions who, as a matter of fact, have the children taken right into the homes of the foster parents in a great many instances. I think my hon. friend will realize that, with the two hundred 'teen age boys and girls whom we might establish, some other plan would have to be adopted, such as an arrangement for two or three years, with provision for some return for the services

rendered by the boy or girl of that age. But for the small children it would be preferable to have them adopted permanently into the home.

I should not like this item to pass without expressing my appreciation of what the minister is doing in this regard. I do not know of anything that will redound more to the credit of the government than this wTork, if proper supervision is exercised, as the minister intimates he is prepared to see shall be the case. I also want to express my great admiration for the work, referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Hanson), of that philanthropic gentleman in Glasgow in bringing these boys to the country. I remember in 1908 or 1909 I had charge as I had had for a few years, of the immigration work in the province of Ontario. This gentleman, a man of considerable means, has made this work his life vocation and to it he has devoted his time, his means and his ability. He is anxious to see that the under-privileged boys in the Old Land get a better chance, and I am glad to know that in the province of New Brunswick he has received such encouragement. When he came out to this country I met him, and I have often wondered how he succeeded in his work. I made close inquiries at the time and found that he had established in Glasgow a home at a large farm where he taught the boys agriculture. They were thoroughly instructed in the business and on being sent out here they were sent to the home that has been mentioned, afterwards being placed in the rural districts. I notice that a great number of the homes referred to by the minister are located in the province of Ontario, and I quite agree that that province is probably as well adapted as any other, if not more so, for taking care of these young people. It is an easy matter, to find out whether proper supervision is being exercised in the homes in which these children are placed, and if it is discovered that such is not the case you may rest assured that a condition of this kind will not continue very long. I am satisfied, however, that the work will be satisfactorily carried on while there is co-operation with the provincial governments, who have already the machinery to take care of the children. I want to express my approval of what is being done in this matter, and I trust that this devoted philanthropist of Glasgow, who has made this his lifework and who is putting his means into it, will receive the encouragement to which he is undoubtedly entitled.

While I am glad to see the government are now taking some some little interest in immigration from the Mother Country-and I sincerely congratulate them upon arousing from the slumber they were enjoying-I would ask my hon. friend what arrangement was made between Great Britain and Australia and New Zealand under which, according to the Associated Press, those dominions secured 11,000 immigrants, and what was the arrangement under which Canada was able to get in the same length of time only 130 immigrants?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend expect an answer?

Certainly. I
am now dealing with the scheme of immigration started by the Mother Country, and if I am wrong I want my hon. friend to interrupt me at once. Under this scheme I ask my hon. friend what the arrangement was with the Mother Country under which Australia and New Zealand got 11,000 immigrants in the period during which we were able to get only 130? Now I hope my hon. friend will understand what I am asking him.
i

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend's arithmetic is correct.
I stood up for correction.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the official figures before me, but is my hon. friend aware-and I think he is-that notwithstanding the fact that Australia has spent huge sums to establish British people there, last year about 86,000 people entered Australia and about 72,000 left? Of course my hon. friend wants to make a comparison between Canada, where we are just beginning a scheme of selected, assisted immigration, and Australia, where they have had the scheme in operation for some time. But if we had secured such a small net gain as has Australia I think my hon. friend might very well criticize us rather severely. He seems to be under the impression that Canada is the only country from which people happen to be migrating, but he is very much mistaken. The Australian immigration scheme has already involved a huge expenditure on assisted passages and the purchase of land for settlers. Speaking for myself personally, I want to approach this question with due caution. I have said upon innumerable occasions that I wish to see people from Great Britain settle in Canada. That is my desire. But when my hon. friend says that 132-

130.

I quite appreciate the fact that my hon. friend does not want to discuss this matter overmuch, that he wants to get off into something collateral, to talk about emigration from Australia. My hon. friend asks me where my particulars came from. The figures were given by the Associated Press. I do not know if they are right. I am not the minister of the department. So this British Empire scheme, so far as Canada was con-

cerned, was a dead letter until the matter was brought to my hon. friend's attention in the House about three weeks ago, when he sent his deputy over.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have never been accused of evolving a scheme so quickly as that. Indeed, the whole current of criticism is that I have been acting too slowly.
I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But I have made a wonderful record upon this occasion if this is all the result of the suggestion of my hon. friend since parliament assembled. However, I am not going to take credit for it. I discussed this matter and sent Mr. Smart to England last fall, as I pointed out to my hon. friend, to look into the situation. I will admit that perhaps I have been cautious. I am not always cautious, and sometimes I have regretted my haste. But I should like to know how successful a scheme of assisted immigration is likely to be. It is all very well to say, "We will vote a big sum of money to bring out a large number of people." But we do not know what we are going to do with them when they come here unless we vote a further sum to establish them upon the land, because I think my hon. friend will agree with me that generally throughout Canada there was not at that time much opportunity for newcomers in the urban centres. There is to-day. To the extent there is such opportunity we will endeavour to place immigrants in our urban centres. But because Great Britain and Australia have joined hands in a scheme of this kind, I do not know that we would be warranted in embarking on such a heavy expenditure as has Australia in connection with it. South Africa seems to be dealing rather carefully with the matter, although they are spending money upon improving their land holdings for the purpose of placing settlers upon them. I want to start in a moderate way. My hon. friend says that 130 people were assisted to Canada.
I do not know. I have quoted the figures given by the Associated Press.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know where they came from. A greater number of young domestic servants came into this country under the assisted passage scheme. My hon. friend knows that people in Montreal, in Saskatchewan, the Ontario government, have been acting in this matter for years, so I hardly know where the 130 would originate; there must have been a much larger number than that. It is important that this matter

should receive careful consideration, and we have given it that consideration. I think we are warranted in asking for the co-operation of the Overseas Settlement Board for this purpose.

The minister has not yet answered my question. If it is an improper question, that is a different matter. Surely the department knows what is being done under this large Empire scheme by the other dominions, and surely it is proper that we should have that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Australia, in addition to assisting the payment of passages -and that applies to adults as well as to children-has a land settlement scheme, a training scheme-they seem to have innumerable schemes involving the expenditure of money in a rather lavish way. But after all, they have not got very many more immigrants than Canada and not nearly as many as the United States. Clearly the Britisher wants to go to Canada because it is closer. My hon. friend knows that the Australian scheme involves a very large expenditure.
I do not. That is why I afn asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: The minister takes a great deal of credit for being cautious; it is quite evident that so far nothing has been done in this matter. I pointed out last night that on three different occasions it has been stated that the government had an immigration policy which was to be put into operation, but we are now informed that no arrangement has so far been made in connection with the overseas settlement scheme. It is a remarkable fact that we are spending much money in the United States to induce immigration from that country and a relatively small amount in the Old Land; and we refuse to co-operate with the British government in establishing their people here.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
WTe did not last session-it may have been our duty to do it-make any proposal to join in a programme of this sort. The matter of providing homes

Supply-Immigration
for those who come here is being examined at the moment, and all that remains to be done is to make the arrangement with the overseas government, and that we are endeavouring to do. My hon. friend knows that we must have the money.

It would not be unusual or surprising for the government to place their plans before parliament in order to justify any expenditure they might subsequently propose in that respect. I noticed a statement in the Globe some 10 p.m. time ago that the Canada Colonization Association were receiving financial assistance from the British government in connection with the scheme discussed here a few days ago. Evidently this company has been making arrangements with the British government with a view to putting into effect the policy which is to be provided for under item 52. Last night I asked the minister what arrangements had been made and he said that that would be discussed under that item. The minister suggests that the money had not been voted and that nothing could be done. But the government need not wait until the money is actually voted before formulating their plans. We ought to know exactly what the British government propose and what the arrangements under consideration are. There appear to be three different plans, one in respect to domestic servants, one in respect to children, and another for ordinary settlers. I have no doubt that the 130 people who came out here were brought into Canada through the instrumentality of the government of Ontario, which for years has been advancing money to assist deserving settlers. In fact, Ontario was compelled to adopt that method because of the neglect of the federal government in the matter. Homes were obtained for these children in advance, and about four-fifths of them, I believe were located in Ontario. This is the season when immigrants should be arriving here, not months later when the demand will slacken off. We have a party expected to arrive in Toronto next week from the north of Scotland, and an agent of the Ontario Department of Immigration has gone to meet them at the seaboard. Places are already provided for them. There is any number of applications for help in the hands of the department, more than they can possibly supply. Yet the minister informs this House that the plans are not yet completed, and here we are almost into the month of April and the immigrants should be arriving within the next few weeks and be placed on the farms of this particular province at least. I think 94
it shows that the minister, instead of being cautious, has been neglecting the duties that should be discharged by his department. It may be that through pressure of work connected with several other departments he has not been able to devote the time he should to this work, but it is altogether too important a matter to be treated lightly.
When I asked the minister a question a short time ago as to the amount of money that was be'ng spent in the United States and Great Britain, he replied that he had given the figures on several occasions and he wanted me to take them down. Well, I took them down, and before he sat down he had given two different sets of figures, and I found that I was nearer right than he was when he stated that I had taken a wrong view of the situation.
I, do not believe the minister is treating this matter seriously, and I am inclined to believe the House is not being treated in the manner it should be. I am sure the people of this country are looking for something different from the Department of Immigration at this time, owing to the fact that during all the years of the war immigration was practically shut out of this country. It was not natural to expect immigration then, but the result is that to-day the agricultural industry of this country is at a standstill because of the lack of labour on the farms, and there is an abundance of labour to be had for the British government is- willing to assist in this matter. We do not know just how far. We cannot get that information from the minister. I think this matter is altogether too important to be rushed through in this way without the House being given the information to which it is entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This $600,000 vote is divided into three-$200,000 for children, $200,000 for domestics, and $200,000 to be loaned to individuals for passages under a nomination scheme. We expect the British government will agree to all three, because this is practically what they are doing with the Australian government. Indeed, that is their offer, and we have simply devised our scheme so that we will have no difficulty in that respect. I mentioned a moment ago that there did appear to be difficulty developing over selection with the Australian gov-enment. I hope we shall not have that difficulty. That refers entirely to children.
So far as farm labour is concerned, it is coming to every province in Canada, and to every railroad station in Canada. Our department has been receiving for the last three months applications from one end of Canada

Suppl y-I mviigration

to the other from fanners who are willing to hire, preferably by the year. Farm labour is coming forward daily from Great Britain, and some also from the Continent, from Holland and Scandinavia. Every agent of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and every agent of the Canadian National Railways has been an immigration agent for this purpose.
What my hon. friend says about the government of Ontario is very true. I have sought on several occasions to work in co-operation with the provincial governments. That is my desire, and we are working with them to a certain extent, but I do not think we have yet reached that stage of co-operation that will bring real success to an immigration scheme, though I am hoping to reach that stage. I am quite free to .admit that I find an element of suspicion in connection with the federal Immigation department. I do not know why, but I understand that it originated some years ago. So far as I am concerned, my sole desire is for co-operation all round.
As to the children, everything is arranged, except that I am not able to say definitely to-night that we have an agreement with the British government. I hope I shall be able to say that in a day or two because I had a wire to-night which would indicate that matters are almost settled. That is being arranged through Mr. Larkin, the High Com-misioner for Canada in London, in co-operation with the Overeas Settlement Board and Mr. Black, the Deputy Minister, who is over there at the present time.
I should like to deal for a moment with the other phase of the question. The domestic servant problem is one that I endeavoured to arrange in co-operation with the provincial governments. Ontario, as my hon. friend has said, has been spending money for years to bring out domestic servants to this province, and I believe with very fair success. The province of Saskatchewan is also engaged in this work, and has been for some years. The lady who makes the selections in England for Saskatchewan has been employed partly by the federal authorities and partly by the Saskatchewan government. Both these provinces prefer to work as they have been doing in the past. Nova Scotia prepared to utilize the Salvation Army, and New Brunswick-I am speaking from memory -is prepared to do the same thing. Ontario, in spite of the fact that they are bringing out domestics themselves, has also an arrangement with the Salvation Army to bring out domestics. Manitoba has expressed the desire that

the Army might be used for this purpose so far as they are concerned, and so has British Columbia. So far as Alberta is concerned, they do not desire to go into a scheme of this kind at all. The reason I mention these matters is to show that we did endeavour to get the provincial governments to say how many of these young women might find employment in the respective provinces, and where they could be placed, and we sought to get them to assume the responsibility, because this is not a grant; it is a loan, with a ten per cent reduction for losses, for the full amount of the passage.
May I ask what it is proposed to loan in each individual case?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the domestic was coming to Nova Scotia, to Halifax, for instance, her loan would be the cost of her passage to Halifax, and similarly if she were going to Winnipeg. If she were going to British Columbia it would be just that much more. There is a minimum and a maximum that can be loaned, but the amount in each case depends altogether on the destination for which the domestic is bound.
What is estimated to be about the average cost for passage of each individual?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: About $125, taking Winnipeg as a central point.
What arrangement has the government made for the collection of these loans?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am coming to that portion of it, because there is where our difficulties begin.
I thought so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
With a federal organization scattered all over Canada for the collection of the money to be advanced, it would be too cumbersome and too expensive; therefore you can only utilize some responsible organization that is engaged in the work. The provincial governments ot Ontario and Saskatchewan are putting up their mfoney. They are taking their own chances of collection, and making their own selection. Although the province of Saskatchewan at one time showed a desire to join us in this scheme, so far none of the provinces is prepared to go into it, and I am not sure that, so far, we have any organization of a responsible character prepared to come forward and say they will re-pay 90 per cent of the advance, except the Salvation Army, and they are recognized by the Overseas Settlement Board. I hope

Supply-Immigration
that we shall later be able' to get a responsible organization that will give a guarantee of that sort. The Salvation Army have carried on with the Ontario government, and have given satisfaction, so far as I can find out. I inquired of the Hon. Manning Doherty, as to the results they had had in the collection of the moneys advanced to the Army, and he told me they had had splendid results and that the system relieved the government of the responsibility of making the collections of the moneys advanced. There is no doubt that there will be other organizations which would undertake this work, but so far the Salvation Army is the only organization that is able to meet the requirements and satisfy the Overseas Settlement Board, because in this particular case, so far as they are concerned, I want the committee to realize that the Overseas Settlement Board, whether money is advanced by way of a loan, expect the federal government of the country to which a person is emigrating to repay that loan, or whatever portion 'of that loan is collected, on a fifty-fifty basis. So far as the Army is concerned, they are making a division, the Army paying one-third, the domestic herself, or the individual, where they are dealing with males, one-third and the government one-third. So far as we are concerned, we will have to put up 50 per cent. In this particular case the Overseas Settlement Board would put up the other 50 per cent, and they guarantee to return 90 per cent of the loan. That is the guarantee they offer as a responsible organization.
To make that clear, the guarantee is given by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: By the Salvation Army.
Not by the association that puts up the 50 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No; the
Overseas Settlement Board is quite prepared to have the Army responsible for their contribution, to repay it to them if we so desire. There is just that one difference. They have expressed the willingness if we so desire, if any advances are made to the Army, to accept the army as the responsible medium for repayment. That would, of course, reduce the risk very materially. That is the only organization that we have at the moment to deal with, in so far as domestic servants are concerned. I hope we will be able to get some other responsible organizations to engage in this work, because as near as we can estimate the amount, 5,000 domestic servants could be placed in Canada if they could be procured. 94 i
One difficulty is that there seems to be so many occupations in Canada into which these young women can enter, that they do not remain very long in the homes to which they come in Canada. The other scheme I have in mind is the nominated scheme of passage.

In regard to the domestics that are to be brought out. I understand the shipping authorities will look after the girl3 or domestics on board ship, but that when they get on the train in Canada, no such provision is made in regard to their food. Who looks after that end of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A conductress accompanies every unaccompanied young woman; if arrangements are made that they travel in groups, we send a conductress right through to Vancouver. That has been done for two or three years.

When I travelled on one of the Transcontinental trains some time ago, I noticed about thirty young women, English, Scotch and Irish. The young woman who looked after them went into the Pullman and had her meal. I would expect that, but I passed time and again through the colonist car, where the girls were located, and I found they were eating in any style. There did not seem to be any practical provision made for their meals. These girls coming to this country would not know what provision to make for their meals, and I was wondering if the conductress was responsible for them, and whether, when you got thirty girls of'that description, travelling in a colonist car, three nights on the train, any provision was made that they should be kept separate? Because there are no proper beds and they sleep on slats.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The purpose for which the conductress is appointed and paid is to see to the protection of these young women, and land them at the various hostels provided in every province in Canada now. That is the sole purpose of having a conductress accompany these young women If they are neglectful of their duty we would be glad to hear it.
I did not mean to suggest that. Does the department look after the food situation, or do they have to provide it themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The government has not been bringing these girls out.
I understand the Saskatchewan government, for example, in nearly every case has someone to whom the girl is going. In many cases an advance is made by the individual himself
Supply-/ mmigration

the farmer or the businessman. He sends $160 or $170, brings out the young woman and she is placed in his home. If he has not the money the government in many cases finds it for him. The federal authorities have been given the services of these conductresses and they assemble the girls at the immigration halls in parties of not less than eight, usually up to thirty or forty, and travel right across Canada with them.
Dealing with the nominative scheme, it is the most difficult thing, I think hon. gentlemen will agree, to hold the young man. I have looked into this question and I may say, in answer to my hon. friend from Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) that I have thought very seriously of offering assistance to many of these young Scotch labourers who are quite prepared to come to Canada, but have not the means to pay their passage. But the great difficulty is that these young men will possibly move out. There is nothing that will hold them if they are not satisfied, and you lose touch with them and, perhaps, lose the money that you advance for their passage. Some scheme may be devised of bringing the unattached man out and keeping him in the country, because there are in the Old Land numbers of young men who could be brought out and successfully established in Canada. We have adopted a scheme of asking the farmer here, because this applies only to the farmer, to nominate someone that he knows in the Old Land. We ask that either he or the man who is coming, contribute 25 per cent of the cost of bringing the man out. In 99 cases out of a hundred, practically, these nominations will be of married men with families whose friends are desirous of bringing them out to Canada. In many cases the nomination will be of the wife and family of a man already here. We have decided on rather a simple scheme for the purpose of securing the return of the money. In the first place, the nominator puts up 25 per cent of it. He gives a bond, upon which we expect him to get the name of at least another responsible party, for the repayment of the loan in one year if it is for two persons, that is a man, his wife and a small child, or in two years, if the family is larger, the loan being without interest. That is the scheme we have in connection with nominated passages. We have made arrangements with the Bankers' Association that we shall send the forms upon which to make application to local banks in every community, and they will attend to the collection free of charge. Briefly, that is the scheme that we have to offer for the other $200,000, and it seems 
to me that it is safe. I feel that I am warranted in asking for a trial of it, and I think it will bring here people who will settle permanently, because they are being brought by their friends who are vitally interested in them, and in that case they are more liable to remain in that particular locality or to settle down permanently in our midst.

I do not think any
risk is being taken. The chief objection I have is that nothing is being done. I refer to an article which appeared in the press in September last which I now have in my hand to this effect:
The Peopling of Canada
The Canadian people will approve both the aim and method of the federal government's new immigration policy, etc. The services of the Canadian Colonization Association, an organization backed by private capital, which has been a long time mapping out the field for immigration to this country and will have the financial support of the Imperial government, will be employed in the location of settlers.
Is this the government's policy or is it not? This has been published in the press of this country and it has not been denied. If this other organization is the medium through which immigration into this country is going to be solicited, and we are just being led to believe that something is going to be done by the government, we should have a little understanding with regard to item 53 before this one is passed. This seems a most remarkable state of affairs when we are passing votes for agencies, for salaries of immigration agents. I brought this to the minister's attention last night, and I was told that it had absolutely nothing to do with the other association; yet the very fact that this $200,000 is to be devoted to advancing loans to enable settlers to come to this country, leads me to believe that there is something we have not so far' been made acquainted with. I should like the minister to inform the committee whether this article which I have read has any foundation or not, and whether any advances have already been made to the Canada Calonization Company to bring settlers to this country.
What paper was that?

This was published in the Toronto Globe of September 12, and it has not been contradicted so far as I know. I find that ever since that time the same paper has announced that another immigration policy was being advanced by the government. Surely we are not asked to wait at this time of the year, almost the hegin-

Supply-Immigration
ning of April, for the government to formulate and to put into effect a policy to bring immigrants into this country for the present year. It is simply a matter of waiting to see what is going to happen. Under ordinary circumstances, it would be well to exercise some of the caution to which the minister has referred; but there is no risk to be run as regards the domestic servants who have been referred to. The provincial governments through the hostels which they have throughout the country, have all the machinery, and there is no risk to be run as regards advances made to domestic servants. Ontario has been doing this for years, and it will not entail a cent of expense on the government to do this work. My hon. friend referred to domestics who have been coming out here and asked whether anyone was in charge. Those who come into Ontario are met at the port of landing; they are taken care of until they enter their homes, and after that certain control is kept over them and a close touch is kept with what is going on. If the government are not prepared to act, then they should lend assistance to the provincial government to do something. They should not force the provincial governments to do all the work along this line, and then endeavour to claim some of the credit. The government, from the minister's own admission to-night, are doing absolutely nothing, and I believe from reports published broadcast throughout this country, that another company which is being subsidized by the government is engaged in this work and is now receiving similar grants from the Imperial government. Has any money been advanced to this Canadian Colonization Company up to the present time? That is a fair question; it is a question which is pertinent to the item before the committee. I am sorry that I have to leave in order to catch my train, but I think we deserve some information as regards the question which I have submitted. I want to know whether any arrangement has already been completed by the Canada Colonization Association with the British government to receive financial assistance in order to bring settlers to this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will remember that the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Shaw) asked the question two weeks ago with respect to the matter that he has mentioned.
I did not hear it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The question was answered: "Yes, the Canada Colonization Association got $40,000 from the government last October."
That has nothing to do with the $600,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not a thing.
Then why waste time discussing it?

My hon. friend is very much concerned about wasting time, and I hope he will continue to exercise his caution in that regard. The question I asked was what arrangement had been made between the Canada Colonization Association, which is subsidized by this government and which the minister informed the committee he was keeping in close touch with to earmark every move they were making, so that no advantage could be taken of the government, and the Imperial government to receive financial assistance, as intimated by the newspaper article which I have read.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have already answered my hon. friend.
But he is referring to the Imperial government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know if they have made an arrangement with the Imperial government. I know that they are simply working in the United States.

This is the newspaper which represents the government in this province. The editorial which I refer to has this heading:
The Canadian people will approve both the aim and the method of the federal government's new policy.
This is the heading, and the report goes on to state:
The services of the Canada Colonization Association-an association backed by private capital-which has been a long time mapping out the field for immigration to this country and which will have the financial support of the Imperial government, will be employed in the location of settlers.
This is the newspaper article that has led the people of the country to believe that this association was engaged in this work, and the minister tells us now that he has no definite information regarding the matter. The deputy minister is in the Old Country, but surely the minister can keep in touch with events over there. Are we simply putting these items in the estimates to make it appear to the people that the government propose some time to do something along this line, but that in the meantime they have no in-
Supply-Immigration

tention of doing anything? If that is the case I think it would be better to say so now and end the farce.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have been trying all evening to tell my hon. friend what we were doing. At one stage of the proceedings he seemed quite favourable, but now he appears to have a different attitude altogether. I am extremely anxious to carry out what I have suggested to-night, and I thought I was going to have the support of my hon. friend, but apparently he does not desire me to get on with the attempt I am making to have the arrangement completed in the Old Land. I am very anxious to bring people from the Old Country into Canada, and I have spent considerable time to-night explaining to the committee what we are doing. I hope I made myself clear, because I certainly did want to put the position fully before the committee. At one stage my hon. friend was quite enthusiastic; he said, "Here at last is something upon which I can agree with the minister." But unfortunately I have spoiled it all by explaining too much.

The minister has certainly devoted a good deal of time to informing the House as to what he has not done, but as regards anything having been done, I fail to see what results have been obtained through the policy that has been featured in the press so often during the last few months.

My criticism of the minister s policy will not be of the character offered by the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland). He has criticized the minister in one breath for not having done anything, and, in the next breath, for spending money on the Canada Colonization Association. If I have any criticism to offer it is because the minister has paid over money to this association before it has been voted by parliament. I fully approve of the policy of not making any agreement that calls for an expenditure of public moneys until it is voted by parliament, and I am glad that the minister has been exercising some caution in this respect. I do take strong exception to money being paid to this association. I do not approve of the scheme at all. However, I did not rise at this moment to make any speech on this point. I simply want to endorse what has been said by my leader (Mr. Forke) earlier in the evening, and to suggest that the minister give the items in connection with this vote of $600,000. I would ask him to put those items on Hansard so that we may be able to con-

sider them beforehand. My IeadeT asked that this item, together with item 53, be allowed to stand that the details be put on Hansard, and I should like to defer any further remarks in coneetion with these votes so that the minister might have an opportunity to comply with the hon. member's request.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The whole
item covers some $1,700,000, and I think I may justly plead fatigue. I have had a fairly strenuous day and it would take a considerable time to give those items. If the leader of the House (Mr. Mackenzie King) will permit me, I shall be glad to do it on Tuesday.

We all want to save the minister as much as we can. Would it not be easier to have the details drawn up and a copy sent to the hon. member (Mr. Forke) and to anyone else who might want it? I have tried to follow the minister as closely as possible. As far as I can understand him, in connection with the first item of $200,000, in so far as our financial commitments are concerned, the British government puts up 50 per cent and we 50 per cent, and both say good-bye to it. In regard to the next item, the domestics, that also is something that is handled entirely in co-operation with the British government. They are to be responsible for 50 per cent, and we for 50 per cent. But there is in connection with that a further qualification. The British government's share is to be repaid before we get ours, unless we make an arrangement with the Salvation Army and substitute them for ourselves so that we shall have no further responsibility for the 50 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
There remains, however, a third class which I understood my hon. friend to say the home government had nothing to do with.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes.

Then I misunderstood my hon. friend, because it seemed to me that we were putting up money for the nominator, on the bond of the nominator, on the payment of 25 per cent in cash. I did not understand that the British government had anything to do with this.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Then the whole of the vote depends on the making of an agreement with the British government. I should like to know whether a draft agreement has yet been prepared, so that we may have some idea of its contents.

Supply-Immigration

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, we have not yet got a draft agreement with the British government; that will have to be entered into. I am waiting for particulars to know what form that draft will take.

I notice further that for the purposes of the agreement we are to have regulations. I wonder whether my hon. friend could not give the committee some idea as to what regulations he will adopt for the purposes of assisting and helping the immigrant, on the one hand, and protecting the country, on the other. The whole thing is to be done by way of regulations. Does he propose new regulations? Is so, in what connection does he need anything new?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is very little needed. I regret that I did not before inform the committee that we expect the Overseas Settlement Board to join in the third scheme. That is the hope but there will be this difference in connection with it, that we shall be responsible for the whole amount. Of course it will be divided between the Overseas government and the federal government of Canada, but we shall be responsible for the repaymnt of the whole amount. That is the difference between the domestic scheme and that of the nominated passage. But it is only on account of the Salvation Army that we escape the responsibility for the half furnished by the British government in the scheme for bringing out domestics. The regulations are much along the lines that I have explained. Arrangements have been made with the banks, and they understand what we propose doing. As these bonds come in properly filled out we send them forward.

Just a word further in regard to putting a detailed statement be-for us so we may have an opportunity to consider it during the week end. Practically every member is on two or three committees, some of which are sitting twice a day, and it is only on Saturdays and Mondays that we have a chance to attend to anything outside that work. For this reason I hope the minister will give us, even although it be only in brief outline, particulars of the items under which the $1,800,000 will be spent. Unfortunately most of the Progressive members are from the extreme ends of the Dominion and do not go home over the week end, so they will be here and in a position to study these particulars. If the minister adopts this suggestion I am sure it will expedite the passage of these items.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I had in mind that hon. members would be having a week's rest. -
We would like an opportunity to consider these particulars before Monday afternoon if possible. Could the minister not give us a brief outline of the expenditures?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are
innumerable.
All we want is a brief outline of the heads under which the $1,800,000 will be spent.
Does the minister intend to go on with this next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should like to have the assisted passage scheme disposed of, because until it is settled I am unable to say definitely to the British government whether we can begin or not.
If the minister does not intend to go on with it next week he could put the items on Hansard later.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can put them on to-night.
As we have had a pretty full explanation regarding the $600,000 vote I would suggest that it be passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would
facilitate business very much if the committee would agree to let it pass.

I do not think I could agree to that, Mr. Chairman. I should like to have a little more information as to the form of the agreement and the regulations. I would point out to my hon. friend that the way the vote is worded leaves a doubt as to whether he would make his arrangements for nominated passages through the British government. He hopes to, but he is not at all sure about it. At the same time he wants to do business. If he takes his vote this way he cannot do it apart from the agreement. I think he had better consider very carefully whether he wants the bargain in that form.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I had Mr. Edwards draw this agreement after careful consideration of the Overseas Settlement Act. He drew it as best he could in conformity with the act.

If the minister does business under the overseas scheme entirely the agreement is perfectly well drawn. I understood that my hon. friend was going
Interim Supply

to do business under that act as far as children and domestics are concerned, but beyond those classes he was not quite determined how to proceed.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh yes, I have no intention of using any part of this money except in conjunction with the Overseas Settlement Board.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.
I do not think there is any particular hurry for putting the particulars on Hansard to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot very well give a summary without using all these sheets, involving several hundred names and the amounts mentioned for printing and advertising, in Great Britain $202,000 and in the United States $370,000 if I remember correctly, and a great many other items. Would it be satisfactory to the committee if I prepared a statement of the amounts spent on salaries and advertising and lumped these together? Otherwise it will mean a great deal of detail.
If the minister is preparing a statement why not set out the information in detail? It will be quite easy to do so.

If we could get an intelligent grasp of how these moneys are being spent we would be satisfied. It would facilitate the business of the committee if we had this information beforehand.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before the adjournment may I call the attention of the House to the fact that we are on the edge of a new fiscal year, and though we have made considerable progress with the Estimates the supplies are not in a condition to warrant us making anything like an extensive appropriation. I am going to ask the House on Monday, if I can obtain unanimous consent, for a special supply bill covering two months of the coming year. I give notice in this informal way in the hope that the House will agree to it without division.
On motion of Mr. Fielding the House adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
Monday, March 26, 1923
